title: Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley Demand Investigation into ICE Tire Slashing Incident
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01) and Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley demanded an investigation into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents for slashing a couple’s tires in Hillsboro.

The couple was observing and recording ICE agents in a supermarket parking lot on October 7, 2026, before multiple masked ICE agents in three vehicles tailed the couple, boxed them in, and repeatedly stabbed and slashed their tires before driving away. A video of the incident can be viewed here.

“ICE agents cannot act with impunity,” the lawmakers wrote. “The First Amendment protects the right to observe, gather information, and record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public. These constitutional protections are necessary for the public to learn about and freely debate the government’s actions, including potential misconduct, and demand accountability when necessary.”

The lawmakers noted that there have been many documented cases of excessive use of force and intimidation tactics against peaceful community members and legal observers by ICE in Oregon and across the country. They called for the Inspector General for the Department of Homeland Security to immediately investigate the Oct. 7 incident in Hillsboro, identify the agents involved, and preserve all evidence, so that those responsible may be disciplined.

“Without videos from bystanders, observers, journalists, and protestors, the public would never know the full scale of federal retaliation against those who seek to document ICE activity,” the lawmakers wrote.

Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley, and Dexter also recently raised concerns about the lack of access to counsel for individuals detained by ICE and what appear to be new protocols for bypassing the Portland ICE facility entirely. That letter can be found here.

The full letter about the Oct. 7 incident can be read here and below:

Dear Inspector General Cuffari:

We write to request an investigation into an alarming incident that occurred on October 7, 2026, in which U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents harassed, intimidated, and retaliated against a couple in Hillsboro, Oregon for engaging in First Amendment activities. The incident occurred when our constituents observed and recorded ICE agents in a supermarket parking lot. Soon thereafter, multiple masked ICE agents in three vehicles recklessly tailed the couple, boxed them in, and dangerously vandalized their vehicle by repeatedly stabbing and puncturing one of their tires before driving away.1

ICE agents cannot act with impunity. The First Amendment protects the right to observe, gather information about, and record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public.2 These constitutional protections are necessary for the public to learn about and freely debate the government’s actions, including potential misconduct, and demand accountability when necessary.

Since President Trump returned to office in January 2025, federal ICE agents across the country have repeatedly failed to respect rights afforded under the Constitution, especially the First Amendment. We have seen many documented cases of excessive use of force and intimidation tactics by ICE in Oregon, including federal agents needlessly deploying tear-gas and other projectiles against peaceful community members as well as driving erratically and verbally threatening legal observers. This pattern of irresponsible and illegal behavior from federal agents is also evident across the country. For example, federal agents in Memphis, Tennessee harassed observers by swerving at them, tailing them, boxing them in, and pulling them over without reasonable suspicion; sitting outside of their homes; and assaulting and arresting them.3 In Los Angeles, federal agents fired crowd control weapons into the heads and other sensitive areas of observers, journalists, and protestors. A judge later granted an injunction against this behavior4 and found that the plaintiffs have plausibly alleged that DHS had a policy of retaliating against people who record the activities of agents.5

Most troubling, federal immigration agents killed Alex Pretti while he was peacefully recording and protesting ICE’s actions.6 Through all of this, the Trump administration has repeatedly covered up officer misconduct and obstructed investigations.7 To this day, there is no evidence that the federal government has meaningfully investigated Mr. Pretti’s killing, with his parents noting that “at every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers.”8 This reckless behavior and senseless violence endangers everyone across the country and does not advance ICE’s mission of enforcing immigration laws to preserve national security and public safety.

Without videos from bystanders, observers, journalists, and protestors, the public would never know the full scale of federal retaliation against those who seek to document ICE activity.

We hereby demand that your offices immediately undertake an investigation of the October 7, 2026, incident in Hillsboro, Oregon outlined above. Please identify the ICE agents involved and preserve all relevant evidence so the officers can be disciplined and prosecuted as appropriate.

Further, we request that you undertake a comprehensive investigation of the pervasive pattern of ICE agents acting unlawfully and retaliating against individuals exercising their First Amendment rights. We ask that you work with Congress to make lasting changes to ICE training, oversight, and accountability. The rights of our constituents must not be jeopardized any longer.

Sincerely,

###

title: Oregon Delegation Celebrates Federal Support for Oregon’s Hazelnut, Seafood Industries
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Oregon’s U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley led Oregon Congressional Delegation members—including Senator Ron Wyden and U.S. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Val Hoyle (OR-04), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), and Janelle Bynum (OR-05)—to announce that after pressure from the delegation, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) will purchase hazelnuts and Pacific Whiting fillets under the agency’s Section 32 purchase program. These purchases will benefit communities and rural economies across Oregon by supporting domestic production and distribution of these agricultural goods during periods of significant market disruption and economic uncertainty.

“Our fisheries and farms deliver incredible products all around the world and are the lifeblood of our communities,” said Merkley, who led the Oregon delegation in pressing USDA to include hazelnuts and whiting in its latest food purchase. “This announcement ensures Oregon’s harvesters, processors, and producers will receive critical financial assistance needed to continue operating and providing services here in Oregon and beyond. I am elated the USDA has decided to make these purchases—this is a win for communities across our state.”

“Iconic state industries like agriculture and fishing count on the U.S. Department of Agriculture to do its job and support Oregonians working hard to keep producing their world-class goods,” said Wyden. “I’m glad the full-court press from the delegation has unlocked this win for Oregonians fishing Pacific whiting and growing hazelnuts.”

“Oregonians know that hazelnuts and seafood are some of the state’s most popular and delicious products,” said Bonamici. “Our growers and producers work tirelessly and bolster the local economy. I’m glad the USDA is making this investment.”

“These investments from the USDA will support the people who harvest, process and bring Pacific Whiting fish and hazelnuts to market,” said Hoyle. “By putting Oregon fishermen and farmers first, we’re boosting our coastal and rural economies."

“Oregon’s specialty crop growers are the backbone of our economy, but too many are struggling with rising costs and uncertain markets,” said Salinas. “In the Willamette Valley, generations of farmers have depended on the hazelnut industry for their livelihoods. That’s why I joined my colleagues in pushing USDA to purchase Oregon hazelnuts and Pacific whiting. These purchases will provide much-needed support for our growers and fishing communities while putting more Oregon-grown and Oregon-caught food onto kitchen tables. I’m proud we secured this win for Oregon producers, and I’ll keep fighting to make sure our specialty crop farmers have the markets and resources they need to succeed.”

"Oregon’s farmers and fishermen work hard to feed our communities, and they deserve a federal government that stands behind them,” said Dexter. “Our delegation pushed USDA to act, and these $34 million in purchases will support Oregon’s hazelnut growers and fishermen during a difficult economic stretch. This investment will help sustain local jobs, strengthen rural and coastal economies, and get nutritious food to families who need it.”

“Our farmers are putting in the work every day to keep Oregon families fed,” said Bynum. “And they’re not just helping put food on the table, they’re keeping money with our families, creating good jobs close to home, and giving people what they need to put down roots here in Oregon. Money back in our state and with our farmers is a win-win.”

Previously, Merkley and the Oregon delegation pressed the USDA to include Pacific whiting and Oregon hazelnuts, which account for 99 percent of hazelnuts produced in the United States, in this year’s Section 32 purchases. Following their efforts, the USDA announced it was purchasing $22 million in hazelnuts and $12 million in Pacific whiting.

title: Salinas, Bonamici, Merkley, Wyden Secure over $500,000 for Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District
text:
Tualatin, OR — Today, Congresswomen Andrea Salinas (OR-06) and Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), alongside Oregon Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, announced they secured the release of over $530,000 in federal funding from the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) to support Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District (TSWCD).

In 2022, TSWCD applied to the NRCS for funding to improve fish habitat in Washington County. This work included replacing deteriorated culverts with bridges and modern culverts that help threatened species like steelhead trout move through local waterways. In February 2024, NRCS approved and obligated $1,074,887 to reimburse TSWCD for their work.

As of early September 2026, NRCS had only paid $543,837 of the over $1.07 million they had promised to TSWCD. This $531,000 shortfall has severely challenged TSWCD’s budget and would have stuck the taxpayers of Washington County with the bill. Following outreach from the Oregon delegation, NRSC honored its commitment and released the final sum to TSWCD.

“When Oregonians make a promise, we keep it. The federal government should be held to the same standard,” said Rep. Salinas. “Tualatin Soil and Water did the work to improve our waterways, and Washington County taxpayers should never have been left holding the bag. I’m glad we got this money out the door and where it belongs.”

“Supporting threatened species and their habitats reflects Oregon values and our commitment to environmental protection, and I was grateful when the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District secured federal funds to improve fish habitat in Washington County,” said Rep. Bonamici. “Unfortunately, the Trump administration paid only about half of the promised funding, leaving Washington County taxpayers to pick up the balance. I’m glad that my colleagues and I were able to help resolve this issue and secure all the funds the water conservation district needed for the project."

“Thanks to our efforts, this funding is finally moving forward and will help ensure the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District can continue its work to improve waterways in Washington County,” said Sen. Merkley. “Oregon’s native fish are the lifeblood of our state, supporting the health and vitality of our communities, local economies, and Tribes who have been here since time immemorial. I’ll keep pushing to secure the necessary federal funds to protect our state’s ecosystems for generations to come.”

“I’m glad the full-court press by the delegation unlocked these resources promised by the federal government to the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District,” Wyden said. “These funds will keep waterways improvements on track, helping with water quality and fish habitat alike in Washington County.”

“The Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District much appreciates Congresswoman Salinas and her staff for their work in helping the District receive payment from the U.S. Department of Agriculture for a successful fish habitat project in the Gales Creek watershed of Washington County,” said Dean P. Moberg, Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District Treasurer. “We were impressed with the staff's quick understanding of the payment problem we faced, and we are grateful for the Congresswoman's exceptional response. The letter Congresswoman Salinas provided, along with Congresswoman Bonamici and Senators Merkley and Wyden, was surely instrumental in cutting through red tape and securing the payment of over one half million dollars in federal assistance that had been held up for this project. This payment will greatly facilitate the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District's work in helping residents of Washington County conserve natural resources with voluntary and locally led projects.

title: Balint, Warren, Colleagues Demand Answers from McDonald’s on Whether AI Pricing Tools are Raising Prices and Facilitating Collusion
text:
Text of Letter (PDF)

Washington, D.C. — Representative Becca Balint (VT-AL), a member of the House Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust and U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) demanded answers from McDonald’s President and CEO Chris Kempczinski about how the company generates AI-driven pricing recommendations, whether McDonald’s pressures franchisees to follow them, and how the company assesses the technology’s potential harm to consumers and competition. The letter came after reports that the company is using artificial intelligence (AI) to determine the “optimal price” for individual menu items at each of its locations and pushing franchisees to adopt these AI-based prices.

“We are concerned that McDonald’s may be using AI to squeeze consumers into paying higher prices, and that its AI pricing tools may facilitate collusion between franchisees who should be operating as competitors,” wrote the lawmakers.

U.S. Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.), and Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.) also signed the letter.

According to recent reports, McDonald’s has developed an AI-based pricing tool that it may be using to recommend specific prices for each individual store, building off the massive trove of consumer data that Amazon has collected through its loyalty program and mobile app. For example, two McDonald’s-operated restaurants just two miles apart in Fresno, California reportedly charged prices that differed by as much as 21 percent for the same menu items. The lawmakers raised particular concerns about McDonald’s use of AI-based pricing at a time when food prices are rising nationwide and particularly at McDonald’s. One report found that certain McDonald’s menu prices doubled between 2014 and 2024, rising more than three times as fast as overall inflation and driving away customers who previously relied on McDonald’s for an affordable meal.

“We are concerned that McDonald’s is using its extensive consumer data and algorithmic pricing tools to unfairly raise prices on consumers who are already struggling with high food and dining costs,” wrote the lawmakers.

The lawmakers also questioned McDonald’s for reportedly putting pressure on franchisees to adopt its pricing recommendations, including through new business standards and potential consequences for franchise renewals. They warned that encouraging competing franchisees to rely on a shared pricing tool informed by nonpublic data could undermine independent pricing decisions and raise antitrust concerns.

“While McDonald’s asserts that using data and analytics to inform pricing is a standard business practice, pressuring competing franchisees to use a shared AI pricing tool built on nonpublic data is not a standard business practice, but rather a potential antitrust issue,” continued the lawmakers.

The lawmakers requested answers by November 16, 2026, on the data and algorithms used to generate pricing recommendations, the extent to which franchisees adopt those recommendations, the pressure McDonald’s places on franchisees to comply, and the company’s assessment of potential antitrust risks.

text:

Early ballots must be received by 7 p.m. MST today, and the recommended mailing date has passed. Voters who still have one should instead sign and date the envelope, then return it to any voting location in their county.

title: Harshbarger Applauds Historic Trump Administration Action to End Hidden PBM Fees and Increase Transparency
text:
Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Diana Harshbarger (R-TN), Vice Chair of the Subcommittee on Health of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, released the following statement applauding the U.S. Department of Labor’s (DOL) final rule cracking down on hidden pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) fees. Under the rule, PBMs — the middlemen that manage prescription drug benefits — and their affiliated brokers must give employers that fund their own workers’ health plans a written breakdown of all the money they expect to make. That breakdown is due both when a contract is signed or renewed and every six months afterward. Employers also get the right to audit those numbers to make sure they are accurate:

“Where there's mystery, there's margin, and PBMs have made a fortune off both,” said Congresswoman Diana Harshbarger. “As a pharmacist for decades, I've watched these shadowy middlemen pad their pockets at the expense of patients, employers, and the community pharmacies that serve them. Employers footing the bill for their workers' healthcare have been kept in the dark about how PBMs really make their money. Thanks to President Trump and Secretary Sonderling, those days are over. Employers will finally see the hidden rebates, fees, and markups PBMs pocket — and they'll have the right to audit the books. That means better deals, lower prescription drug costs, and more money back in the pockets of American workers and their families.”

“This is a win for every American worker who has ever paid too much at the pharmacy counter,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “For years, PBMs have operated in the shadows, pocketing hidden fees while workers and employers were left in the dark. Today, President Trump is delivering the transparency Americans deserve – and putting American workers first.”

“More transparency means more competition, and more competition means lower health care costs,” said Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “Today’s new rule represents a significant step forward in this Administration’s all-of-government effort to take the guesswork out of shopping for health care – an effort in which Labor, CMS, and numerous other agencies and departments all have important roles to play.”

BACKGROUND:

On November 2, the U.S. Department of Labor finalized a rule of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), the federal law that governs employer-sponsored health plans. The rule requires PBMs — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and run prescription drug benefits for health plans — to disclose to employers exactly how they get paid. It covers large employers that pay for their workers’ healthcare directly instead of buying coverage from an insurance company. It also applies to the brokers and consultants tied to PBMs. President Trump first directed the Labor Department to propose stricter transparency rules in his April 15, 2025, executive order, “Lowering Drug Prices by Once Again Putting Americans First.”

Under the rule:

PBMs must give employers a written breakdown of all the money they expect to make from their contract — when the contract is signed or renewed, and every six months after that, or every three months if the employer asks.

For the first time, PBMs must disclose three major sources of hidden profit:

Rebates and other payments from drug companies;

The “spread,” when a PBM charges a health plan more for a drug than it pays the pharmacy and keeps the difference; and

Fees PBMs take back from pharmacies after a prescription is filled.

Employers can audit the numbers to make sure they are accurate.

The rule applies to employers with roughly 100 or more employees or plan members.

Self-insured employer health plans cover about 90 million Americans. The Labor Department projects the rule will lower prescription drug costs for plans and participants by as much as $22 billion over 10 years. The rule takes effect January 4, 2027, and applies to plan years beginning on or after July 1, 2027.

Congresswoman Harshbarger championed two bills that laid the groundwork for this rule:

PBM Reform Act: Introduced in July 2025 with Congressman Buddy Carter (R-GA), the bipartisan bill would require PBMs to give employers and patients semiannual reports on drug spending, rebates and formulary decisions, and would decouple PBM compensation from drug prices in Medicare Part D. Provisions of the bill helped shape the PBM reforms President Trump signed into law Feb. 3 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 — the law this rule implements. That law also requires PBMs to pass 100% of manufacturer rebates and fees through to employer plans for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028.

PBM Sunshine and Accountability Act: Introduced in April 2023, the bill would require PBMs to report the rebates and fees they receive from drug manufacturers — including amounts they keep rather than pass through to health plans — and the payments they claw back from pharmacies, and would extend that reporting to employer group health plans. The Labor Department rule now requires PBMs to disclose many of the same categories of compensation directly to employers.

title: Representative Min and Senator Welch Demand Answers from Former Trump Attorney Alina Habba-Mildon on Influence over President’s Pardon of Corrupt Venezuelan Banker Julio Herrera Velutini
text:
Washington, DC. — U.S. Representative Dave Min (D-CA-47), Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ Anti-Corruption Task Force and U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, are demanding answers from former Senior Adviser to the Attorney General Alina Mildon on her reported role in President Trump’s decision to grant Julio Herrera Velutini—who pleaded guilty to violating U.S. campaign finance laws—a full presidential pardon. The letters come as President Trump criticized his former attorney’s $50 million agreement with Mr. Herrera as “totally obnoxious and outrageous,” and “not acceptable.”

In their letters, the lawmakers express concern that the timing of Ms. Habba-Mildon’s hiring and Mr. Herrera’s daughter’s contribution to MAGA Inc. raise questions about whether improper considerations, including quid pro quo or “pay-to-play” dynamics, may have affected President Trump’s decision to pardon him. These letters are part of a broader bicameral investigation led by Representative Min and Senator Welch into potential corruption surrounding President Trump’s decisions to grant presidential pardons.

The lawmakers write: “Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution authorizes the President to ‘grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offenses against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.’ The U.S. Supreme Court has characterized executive clemency as ‘an act of grace’ exercised for the ‘public welfare.’ President Trump’s use of this authority appears to deviate from this traditional purpose. Congress has a compelling interest in ensuring that the constitutional pardon power is exercised with fairness and transparency. Given these circumstances, we are seeking additional information to better understand the extent to which influence and access may have overridden the standard pardon review process.”

In August 2022, Mr. Herrera was criminally charged with providing $300,000 to a super political action committee (PAC) in violation of a campaign finance law barring contributions or donations by foreign nationals to U.S. federal, state, or local elections. Mr. Herrera financially supported the reelection campaign of Puerto Rico’s governor in exchange for her pledge to remove a top banking regulator who had scrutinized one of Mr. Herrera’s banks.

According to public reporting, Ms. Mildon entered into an employment agreement with Mr. Herrera’s family in late 2025, while she was serving as an adviser at the Justice Department. She also previously served as President Trump’s personal lawyer and as the Acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey. In the hiring contract, Mr. Velutini’s family agreed to pay her $50 million over four years to be general counsel at Concord Partners, a company set up by Mr. Velutini’s daughter days before she signed the contract. Ms. Mildon finalized the deal with Concord Partners while she was still serving at the Justice Department.

Ms. Mildon then began working for Concord Partners on January 1, 2026, while serving as a senior adviser to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. Two weeks later, Mr. Herrera received a pardon on January 15, 2026. Since President Trump’s election in November 2024, his 27-year-old daughter, a self-employed financial consultant, also donated $3.5 million to MAGA Inc., a Trump-supporting super PAC.

Read and download the lawmakers’ full letters to Alina Habba-Mildon and Julio Herrera Velutini.

In May, Senator Welch and Rep. Min sent letters to 17 individuals who received pardons or commutations under circumstances that warrant further congressional scrutiny, including several individuals connected to major fraud schemes, financial crimes, and high-profile political or financial relationships tied to President Trump and his associates. The earlier letters sought information regarding the clemency process, including whether financial contributions, lobbyists, intermediaries, or personal connections played a role in securing presidential clemency.

Among the individuals who received letters are convicted fraudsters, political fundraisers, corporate executives, and wealthy donors, such as Changpeng Zhao, whose cases have generated public reporting suggesting unusual access to Trump’s network of political allies and associates, direct lobbying efforts, large political donations, or other concerning connections surrounding their clemency requests.

The lawmakers continued their investigation in June, sending four additional letters to the Department of Justice’s Office of the Pardon Attorney, the White House Office of Records Management, the White House Pardon Czar, and the United States Secret Service. In October, the lawmakers initiated a probe into the influence of cabinet members, U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin, in Trump’s decision to pardon convicted felons.

title: Getting America Building Again
text:
Getting America Building Again

INTRODUCING A BLOG POST SERIES ON THE BIPARTISAN AMERICAN AFFORDABILITY AND JOBS ACT

America’s ambitions to strengthen energy security, reshore manufacturing, and lead the world in artificial intelligence depend on one fundamental capability: our ability to build. Yet regulatory uncertainty, prolonged reviews, and endless litigation have stalled critical infrastructure, driven up costs, and discouraged investment.

Drawing on four decades of private-sector experience, Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) has made permitting reform his top priority since joining the Senate in March. He introduced the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure (AEMI) Act, championed reform in his maiden Senate floor speech, and convened more than 150 stakeholders at a June Capitol Hill forum focused on America’s ability to build and compete.

Now, Congress is poised to meet the moment. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) have put forward the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026. Senator Armstrong has praised this bipartisan agreement for including meaningful reforms that would remove longstanding barriers to building critical infrastructure in this country. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has scheduled a procedural vote for November 9, when Congress returns to Washington—an opportunity to turn months of negotiations into legislative action.

That’s the focus of Getting America Building Again, a new blog series examining how the BAAJA will bring benefits including reducing costs, bringing regulatory certainty, and getting critical infrastructure built. Each installment will answer three questions:

The problem: What’s currently holding America back?

The solution: How would the bill address it?

The support: What are stakeholders across the country saying?

In this inaugural post, we note how the need for permitting reform—and the bipartisan agreement to deliver it—has united an extraordinary coalition spanning industry, utilities, advocacy organizations, and the policy community.

Leading business organizations have rallied behind the legislation. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce mobilized more than 850 organizations for comprehensive permitting reform and endorsed the Senate agreement, calling it “a once-in-a-generation opportunity to fix our broken permitting system.” More than 100 manufacturing and business organizations joined the National Association of Manufacturers in urging Congress to “swiftly pass” the bill, while Business Roundtable, the American Council for Capital Formation, and the Small Business & Entrepreneurship Council issued independent endorsements.

Energy providers and industry associations have also lined up behind the bill. The nation’s consumer-owned utilities, represented by the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) and American Public Power Association (APPA), expressed “strong support” in a joint letter. Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA) endorsed it. Leading clean-energy associations—including the Solar Energy Industry Alliance (SEIA), American Clean Power Association (ACP), Corporate Energy Buyers Association (CEBA), and Advanced Energy United—also jointly urged passage, underscoring the importance of permitting reform to expanding electricity supply and modernizing the grid.

Conservative organizations have mobilized, too. Pacific Legal Foundation led more than 35 groups in sending a letter of support, while Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions and SAFE led a separate 15-group coalition letter. Groups that individually endorsed or publicly expressed support for the legislation include: ACC Action, ClearPath Action, Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions, Club for Growth, Conservative Energy Network, Americans for Prosperity, and Pacific Legal Foundation. Cato Institute’s Travis Fisher and Michael Abi-Nader called it an “excellent set of bipartisan reforms.” Foundation for American Innovation’s Thomas Hochman said that BAAJA would be “if passed, the most consequential energy legislation in decades.”

Support also extends across center-left policy organizations and climate advocates. Bipartisan Policy Center Action, the Breakthrough Institute, and Citizens’ Climate Lobby have endorsed the legislation. Inclusive Abundance Action called it “a huge bipartisan win,” while Chamber of Progress described it as “better than most of us could have predicted.” Third Way welcomed “meaningful progress” toward affordable, reliable electricity, and the Progressive Policy Institute applauded a “major bipartisan breakthrough.” The ACORE called the bill “an essential step” toward accelerating clean energy and transmission, while Ceres also praised its provisions to accelerate infrastructure development and modernize the grid.

Even as some environmental groups oppose the compromise, prominent clean-energy and center-left voices are making the case for passage. Climate investor Tom Steyer appealed directly to fellow progressives: “this is a bill we should support, and I’m asking you to join me.” Third Way’s Josh Freed criticized groups “more interested in obstructing imperfect solutions than working to improve them.” Searchlight Institute’s Jane Flegal and Pavan Venkatakrishnan argued that the bill would help unlock clean-energy construction at scale, while Columbia University’s Jason Bordoff warned that rejecting the deal over its potential benefits for fossil fuels would squander an opportunity to advance energy security, affordability, and clean energy.

The stakes are clear, the support is broad, and Congress has an opportunity to act. In the installments ahead, we’ll examine what’s holding America back, how the bipartisan agreement addresses those obstacles, and why a growing choir of stakeholders are calling for reform.

It’s time to get America building again.

title: Sen. Cruz, Rep. Roy Applaud President Trump’s Approval of Federal Disaster Assistance for Texas Flood Victims
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and U.S. Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas-21) issued the following statements after President Trump approved Individual Assistance (IA) for 20 Texas counties impacted by severe weather and flooding between July 12 and August 4, 2026. The decision follows an appeal submitted by the State of Texas to overturn the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) denial of the state’s request for additional assistance.

The following 20 counties are now approved for FEMA IA: Bandera, Bexar, Comal, Crockett, Dimmit, Frio, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, Kimble, Kinney, La Salle, Maverick, Medina, Real, Schleicher, Sutton, Uvalde, Val Verde, and Zavala.

Sen. Cruz said, “I applaud President Trump for approving additional assistance to families and communities devastated by this year’s catastrophic flooding. Texans have endured unimaginable loss, and this assistance will provide much-needed resources to help families rebuild their lives and communities recover. I was proud to work alongside Congressman Roy to support efforts to deliver this critical assistance to our state, and I thank President Trump for his continued commitment to standing with Texans in their time of need.”

Rep. Roy said, “In light of the double devastation of back-to-back floods, the Trump administration’s offer of additional disaster assistance for Texas is welcomed. This is an important step toward helping affected families and communities rebuild. Texans are resilient, and we will recover and rebuild stronger than ever.”

title: Ernst Names Small Business of the Week, Natural Fertilizer
text:
RED OAK, Iowa – U.S. Senator Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Chair of the Senate Small Business Committee, today announced Natural Fertilizer of Harrison County as her small business of the week. Throughout the 119th Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in each of Iowa's 99 counties.

“Abe Sandquist is a grow getter when it comes to operating a small business,” said Chair Ernst. “Over the course of 20 years, Natural Fertilizer has bloomed into a thriving business that has cultivated over 1,000 relationships with partners and farmers across the Midwestern region.”

Abe Sandquist developed the idea of Natural Fertilizer after spending several years developing nutrient management plans for the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. During his time there, Abe’s work revealed that many agricultural producers did not realize the value of organic nutrients until they received professional guidance on how to effectively use them. Seeing this need, Abe established Natural Fertilizer in 2007, providing consulting services focused on nutrient management.

Since then, Natural Fertilizer has transformed into a full-service operation focusing on the nutrient cycle of organic residuals. Beyond building his business, Abe has remained committed to serving his local community. Abe helped launch Woodbine Iowa’s IGNITE Pathways Program and remains an active member of the Iowa Composting Council, where he continues to bring members of the agricultural industry together through nutrient cycle advocacy.

Stay tuned as Chair Ernst continues to recognize outstanding Iowa small businesses with her Small Business of the Week award.

title: Gillibrand, Schumer Demand Trump Approve Major Disaster Declaration For September Nor’easter
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and Senator Chuck Schumer (D-NY) called on President Trump to approve Governor Hochul’s request for a Major Disaster Declaration following the September 26 and 27, 2026 nor’easter that battered downstate New York. The storm brought coastal flooding and heavy winds to Long Island and New York City, resulting in increased expenditure of state and local resources to help communities recover from the disastrous conditions.

In a letter to President Trump, the senators underscored their support for Governor Hochul’s request for disaster relief, which would unlock Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) resources to help alleviate the financial burden that counties and the state took on to mitigate the impacts of the storm. Governor Hochul’s request included Public Assistance for Nassau and Suffolk Counties and Hazard Mitigation for the entire state.

The senators wrote, “We support the Governor’s request for Public Assistance (PA) for Nassau and Suffolk Counties and Hazard Mitigation for the entire State. We also support the inclusion of any additional counties that New York State believes meets the threshold for PA. Such a declaration under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (P.L. 100-707) would unlock crucial Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) resources.”

The senators continued by emphasizing the disastrous nature of the storm. They wrote, “The storm battered southern New York with strong winds and heavy rain, which combined with a full moon that exacerbated high tides, caused major coastal flooding and flash flooding. In addition to the flooding, gale-force winds felled trees and branches that damaged utility poles. During the storm over 200,000 New Yorkers lost power, of which over half were on Long Island.”

The senators concluded the letter by stressing the need for federal resources to help downstate New York recover from the storm. They wrote, “The New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, in partnership with FEMA Region 2 and Nassau and Suffolk Counties, has documented and validated that the damage and costs from this nor’easter exceed the State’s threshold for a disaster declaration.Without federal support that a Major Disaster Declaration can provide, New Yorkers in Nassau and Suffolk Counties will lose a critical partner in their efforts to recover and prepare for future natural disasters.”

The full text of the letter can be found here.

title: Gillibrand Statement On Trump Administration Plan To Undermine Workplace Protections For Pregnant Women
text:
Today, in light of reporting that the Trump administration plans to scale back job protections for pregnant women enacted as part of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand released the following statement:

“President Trump’s continued attacks on women and families are disgraceful. Now, on top of the sky-high cost of groceries, gas, and utilities, American women will also have to worry about losing their jobs if they need accommodations for pregnancy-related issues or to take care of their reproductive health. This is yet another backwards and shortsighted move by the Trump administration that will weaken our economy, harm our families, and erode our personal liberties.”

In 2022, Congress passed the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which Senator Gillibrand cosponsored, as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023. The law instituted the workplace protections for women affected by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions that are now under threat by the Trump administration. These accommodations can include:

Flexible scheduling for prenatal or postnatal appointments

Additional, longer, or more flexible breaks to drink water, eat, rest, or use the bathroom

Light duty, or help with manual labor and lifting

Temporary transfer to a less physically demanding or safer position

Limiting exposure to hazardous chemicals

Access to a water bottle or food

Leave or time off to recover from childbirth, even for those who don’t qualify for FMLA

Leave or time off for bedrest, recovery from miscarriage, postpartum depression, mastitis, and other pregnancy-related health issues

Providing equipment such as a stool to sit on

Changing a uniform or dress code, like allowing wearing maternity pants

Changing a work schedule, like allowing shorter work hours or a later start time to accommodate morning sickness

Breaks, private space (not in a bathroom), and other accommodations for lactation needs, like adding a lock to a meeting room for private breast milk expression

Remote work or telework

Senator Gillibrand has spent her career in Congress championing women in the workplace. In addition to consponsoring the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, she leads the FAMILY Act, which would establish a national program guaranteeing 12 weeks of paid family and medical leave for every American. She has introduced the FAMILY Act in every Congress since 2013. She also introduced the bipartisan More Paid Leave for More Americans Act, which would establish a competitive grant program for states that provide a minimum of six weeks of parental, caregiving, or medical leave, as well as the Comprehensive Paid Leave for Federal Employees Act, which would expand federal paid leave for federal employees to include 12 weeks of family and medical leave.

title: Kelly, Colleagues Demand Census Bureau Rescind Proposed Rule That Violates Constitution
text:
Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Gary Peters (D-MI), Andy Kim (D-NJ), and 23 bipartisan Senate colleagues demanded that the U.S. Census Bureau rescind a proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from census counts and eliminate questions on race and ethnicity.

In their letter, the senators warn that the exclusion of non-citizens violates the Constitution, which expressly says that the census must count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The Bureau has proposed two methods by which it would exclude non-citizens, both of which would cause undercounts and errors in the census counts.

“We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census. The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the ‘whole number of persons in each state.’ The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services,” the senators wrote.

The letter also describes how the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions would undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws and would degrade the quality of all census data. The compliance of civil and voting rights laws rely on demographic data, and only the decennial census provides accurate and precise data. Additionally, eliminating the collection of race and ethnicity data from the decennial census undermines other federal survey data. Businesses and local governments that depend on such data have said that they would be harmed by this proposed rule.

“In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule ‘deteriorates the accuracy’ of ‘fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation’ because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates,” the senators continued. “The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.”

In addition to Kelly, Peters, and Kim, the letter was also signed by Senators Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Angus King (D-ME), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Patty Murray (D-WA), Jack Reed (D-RI), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Ron Wyden (D-OR).

title: Rosen Joins Nevada Delegation in Calling on IRS to Release Delayed Data on ‘No Tax on Tips’ Impact
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Senator Jacky Rosen (D-NV) joined the Nevada Democratic delegation in a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) urging the release of delayed tax data on the impact of the Trump Administration’s implementation of Republicans’ Big Beautiful Bill. Recent reporting details the IRS’s effort to delay the release of this data ahead of the midterm elections, hiding the true impact that the Republicans’ legislation and its implementation, including “No Tax on Tips,” have had on working families.

“As lawmakers representing our nation’s most hospitality and service-industry-dependent economy, securing tax relief for tipped workers has been a longstanding bipartisan priority for the Nevada delegation,” wrote the Members. “In August of 2025, we sent a letter to Secretary Bessent regarding implementation of the deduction for tipped income, and providing recommendations for its successful implementation and offering our offices as a resource. We remain committed to ensuring this policy succeeds, and obtaining accurate tax data is critical to guiding our continued oversight and support. Without access to the IRS’s statistics, neither Congress nor the public can fully assess whether this deduction for tips is delivering the relief it was designed to provide.”

“We therefore ask the IRS to clarify the cause of these delays and take the necessary steps to ensure the prompt release of any outstanding tax analyses. Please respond as soon as possible. Any further delay in the release of this information or in outlining a plan to do so flies in the face of the IRS’s responsibility to Congress and to the American taxpayer,” concluded the Members.

Read the full letter HERE.

Senator Rosen has consistently fought to lower costs for hard-working Nevadans. She helped introduce and pass the standalone No Tax on Tips Act in the Senate, a bipartisan bill to exempt tips from federal income tax. Senator Rosen has also spoken on the Senate floor, calling for tax relief for hard-working Nevada families. In 2024, she also introduced bipartisan legislation to cut taxes for veterans starting small businesses. Senator Rosen strongly supports raising the federal minimum wage and eliminating the minimum wage gap for tipped workers nationally.

title: NEWS: Schiff Joins Cortez Masto, Democratic Colleagues in Requesting Answers from X On Apparent Preferential Treatment of Polymarket
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) in a letter to X (formerly Twitter) Chief Compliance Officer C. Rob DeCampos requesting answers on the seemingly preferential treatment Polymarket is receiving from X. The Senators raise concern that, due to Donald Trump Jr.’s role as an adviser and investor for Polymarket, any preferential treatment could help the President and his family enrich themselves.

“Typically, X allows users to report an ad for a myriad of reasons; however, when attempting to report Polymarket’s ads through the standard X interface, users are denied the option to do so (Figure A). This is not the case with other types of advertisements, including Kalshi, another prediction markets platform offering sports gaming that is illegal in states across the U.S.,” the Senators wrote.

“This seemingly preferential treatment calls into question whether X is attempting to provide an undue competitive advantage to Polymarket and – by extension – the President and his family,” the Senators continued. “It would not be the first time Donald Trump Jr. has attempted to use his position to enrich himself. Earlier this year, he reportedly pressured a room of Republican state attorneys general to stop trying to regulate prediction markets, which he is heavily invested in.”

The full text of the letter can be found here and below.

Dear Mr. DeCampos,

We bring to your immediate attention concerns that X, formerly known as Twitter, may be giving preferential treatment to Polymarket, a prediction market platform offering illegal sports gambling across the United States. It has been widely reported that Donald Trump Jr., President Donald Trump’s eldest son, is an adviser to and investor in Polymarket. Providing preferential treatment to a specific advertiser with direct financial ties to the President and his family raises significant questions.

Polymarket has been advertising on television, billboards, and social media since resuming limited onshore operations last year. The platform was previously banned in the United States for operating an unregistered derivatives-trading platform and has been the subject of increased scrutiny for enabling fraud and for allowing insider trading that could endanger military operations and national security.

Since the start of the year, Polymarket has also been the subject of lawsuits by state attorneys general for facilitating illegal sports gaming. Since 1961, the Federal Wire Act has prohibited the transmission of bets or wagers through interstate commerce (18 U.S. Code § 1084) and Section 5c(c)(5)(C) of the Commodity Exchange Act permits the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to prohibit event contracts that involve gaming, are unlawful under federal or state law, or are contrary to the public interest.

Despite that, sports wagers on prediction markets – deemed illegal by both the Ninth and Sixth Circuit Courts – make up more than 80 percent of Polymarket’s trading volume and are the primary source of the platform’s rapid growth. Polymarket’s X ads target new users with videos featuring sports betting services and offering financial incentives to create an account.

Typically, X allows users to report an ad for a myriad of reasons; however, when attempting to report Polymarket’s ads through the standard X interface, users are denied the option to do so (Figure A). This is not the case with other types of advertisements, including Kalshi, another prediction markets platform offering sports gaming that is illegal in states across the U.S., including in Nevada (Figure B).

This seemingly preferential treatment calls into question whether X is attempting to provide an undue competitive advantage to Polymarket and – by extension – the President and his family.

It would not be the first time Donald Trump Jr. has attempted to use his position to enrich himself. Earlier this year, he reportedly pressured6 a room of Republican state attorneys general to stop trying to regulate prediction markets, which he is heavily invested in.

Given the need to eliminate even the appearance of impropriety, we request the answers to the following questions:

Does X allow advertisers to purchase ads that cannot be reported through X’s timeline interface?

If so, which advertisers does X provide this service to?

If so, how much additional revenue does X receive for providing this service?

If so, does X receive any preferential treatment from advertisers or regulators for offering this service?

Did Polymarket, its leadership, or any of its representatives approach X about running ads with a limited report function? If so, who?

Did President Donald Trump, Donald Trump Jr., or any other member or representative of the Trump family approach X about running ads with a limited report function? If so, who?

How does X plan to ensure prediction market ads featuring sports are banned from the platform in states following the Sixth and Ninth Circuit decisions that sports event contracts are sports gaming and must be regulated at the state and Tribal levels?

What is X’s ad policy for prediction market companies given the varying legality across the country?

Does X’s partnership with Polymarket influence the way X’s ad policy applies to Polymarket?

If so, please explain how this policy differs from advertisers without a partnership with X.

Does X provide other official partners customized ad policies?

We ask that you provide responses to our questions no later than November 30, 2026.

We hope you and your team take the time to provide a detailed and thorough response. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

title: Van Hollen, Warren Call on SEC to Abandon Counterproductive Deregulatory IPO Agenda Putting Families and Investors at Risk
text:
U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Committee, wrote to Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chair Paul Atkins with concerns that a recent slate of deregulatory proposals purportedly aimed at “making IPOs great again” would reduce transparency, damage investor confidence, and undermine the integrity of America’s capital markets.

In May, Chair Atkins announced an effort to “Make IPOs Great Again” and encourage more companies to “go and stay public.” While the policy initiative aims to reverse the decline in publicly-listed U.S. companies over the past three decades by reducing public-market disclosures and requirements, research shows that deregulation in the private markets is a key reason why fewer companies have gone public. The Senators note that the SEC’s proposals would be counterproductive and risk exacerbating the decline in public companies.

“While we share the goal of revitalizing the public markets and providing more companies with the opportunity to go public, the ill-conceived deregulatory measures you have taken will not revive or sustain a healthy IPO market,” wrote the Senators. “These proposals would ultimately erode the very framework of transparency and investor protections that makes our public markets so appealing to investors the world over.”

“Your proposals posit that the compliance burden of the robust regulations and disclosures required in the public markets is the sole reason that companies choose to stay private,” the Senators continued. “Academic research has repeatedly discredited your theory and found that more – not less – disclosure from public companies can make markets more liquid, is rewarded by investors with greater returns, and associated with larger stock markets. Moreover, research has shown that deregulation in the private markets is a key reason for why companies do not go public.”

“Our capital markets thrive when more companies go public and go public earlier. Transparency and robust disclosure in our public markets facilitates a more trustworthy and efficient market where Main Street investors are more willing to provide capital because they have faith in the integrity of public markets,” wrote the Senators. “Our goal should be bringing as much capital raising as possible into our public markets to provide more growth opportunities for American companies and more wealth-building opportunities for the broadest range of American investors.”

“As the SEC guts regulations protecting investors from untested issuers, the Commission is simultaneously ‘reliev(ing) a significant portion of all publicly traded issuers from making a wide variety of disclosures that they are currently required to provide,’” the Senators continued. “The result of this wholesale rollback of required disclosure requirements would almost certainly increase the level of fraud and raise the cost of capital.”

The Senators requested that the letter be added to the comment file for all four of the SEC’s proposed deregulatory rules.

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Chairman Atkins,

We write to urge the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC,” or “the Commission”) to reconsider its recent slew of proposals to weaken or eliminate longstanding regulations governing publicly traded company disclosures that make American capital markets the envy of the world. Although you claim to want to “Make IPOs Great Again,” the SEC’s specific proposals to deregulate the public company registration and disclosure regime represent an unprecedented attack on investors’ rights to transparency from public companies and threaten to undermine investor protection and market integrity. Your broad deregulatory agenda would compromise the integrity of our capital markets at a moment when Americans are already reeling from spiraling costs and unprecedented corruption in the Trump economy. We urge you to rescind these recent proposals that would put families and investors at even greater risk.

On May 19, you announced an initiative to “Make IPOs Great Again” intended to encourage more companies to “go and stay public.” This agenda purportedly aims to reverse the decline in the number of U.S. public listings over the last three decades, from a peak of over 8,000 in 1996 to roughly 4,000 in 2024. To that end, you promulgated two rulemakings that would allow more than 80% of public companies to provide less disclosure based on their size and would enable virtually any newly public company to immediately raise more capital with “short-form” registration statements previously reserved for large, seasoned companies.

While we share the goal of revitalizing the public markets and providing more companies with the opportunity to go public, the ill-conceived deregulatory measures you have taken will not revive or sustain a healthy IPO market. Instead, the flawed rationale that requiring less disclosure from public companies will motivate more companies to conduct IPOs has been repeatedly debunked. These proposals would ultimately erode the very framework of transparency and investor protections that makes our public markets so appealing to investors the world over. What’s more, the proposals misconstrue the actual root causes of the decline in the IPO market and do nothing to address the real issue: weak regulation in private markets that incentivizes companies to stay private. Requiring less disclosure from public companies will only damage investor confidence and undermine the integrity of American public markets.

Data Suggests Deregulatory Measures Do Not Result in Increased IPOs. The Real Problem is Underregulated Private Markets.

Your proposals posit that the compliance burden of the robust regulations and disclosures required in the public markets is the sole reason that companies choose to stay private. Academic research has repeatedly discredited your theory and found that more – not less – disclosure from public companies can make markets more liquid, is rewarded by investors with greater returns, and associated with larger stock markets. Moreover, research has shown that deregulation in the private markets is a key reason for why companies do not go public. One study shows that Sarbanes-Oxley-era regulations, for example, which increased corporate financial reporting rules and internal controls for public companies, were not the core cause of the declining IPOs after the law’s adoption in the early 2000s. Instead, declines in IPOs were attributed to a changing market environment in which smaller companies had greater profit potential through acquisition channels, not IPOs. Another study attributes the IPO decline to major private market deregulation in the years prior to Sarbanes-Oxley. The reforms expanded the number of investors permitted in private funds that are not subject to comprehensive SEC oversight, among other deregulatory measures such as preempting state regulation of certain private offerings. These reforms ballooned the supply of private capital available to private companies which significantly contributed to companies opting to stay private entirely or stay private for longer.

Expanded opportunities to raise capital with less expense and oversight in the private markets has created a structural disincentive to going public. In other words, it is not that public markets are overregulated, it is that private markets are underregulated, and repeated deregulatory reforms have pulled more and more capital from the public markets into the private markets. Lighter regulatory requirements – such as no obligation to provide investors with financial statements, quarterly reports, material event reporting, or disclosure about executive compensation – have incentivized a growing number of companies to raise capital in the private markets rather than go public. For example, the number of offerings under Regulation D – which provides the most commonly used exemptions from SEC registration requirements allowing companies to raise money without going public – have increased by more than 150% over the last 16 years. In 2009, there were nearly 14,000 offerings and $588 billion in capital raised through Reg D. In 2025, there were more than 34,000 offerings raising nearly $2.4 trillion. And yet, under your leadership, the SEC is not only failing to strengthen guardrails in private markets, it is proposing to dramatically weaken guardrails in public markets.

Like other similar deregulatory efforts in the past, your proposals are unlikely to achieve their stated goal of incentivizing capital raising in our public markets by lowering the bar for transparency from public companies. Weakening regulations for public companies, for example, was the inspiration of the JOBS Act of 2012, which was designed to improve “access to the public capital markets for emerging growth companies” and “seeks to remove impediments for “emerging” public companies by relaxing disclosure, governance and accounting requirements, [and] easing the restrictions on analyst communications.” The bill also included provisions “designed to allow some private companies to defer going public, including provisions raising the threshold for registration under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.” However, the data since 2012 shows that this policy prescription did not consistently increase the number of public companies in the 14 years since. According to a University of Florida study, the market netted 158 new IPOs the year after the JOBS Act passed Congress. Last year, it netted only 90. There has not been a return to 1990’s IPO levels, where the lowest number of net new IPOs per year was 110, and the high was 677 new IPOs. History has already taught us that deregulation in the public markets does not result in major gains in IPOs over a long-time period.

Our capital markets thrive when more companies go public and go public earlier. Transparency and robust disclosure in our public markets facilitates a more trustworthy and efficient market where Main Street investors are more willing to provide capital because they have faith in the integrity of public markets. Conversely, private markets are intentionally limited to a smaller population of highly sophisticated investors because their lack of transparency and regulation increases the risk of fraud and loss. Our goal should be bringing as much capital raising as possible into our public markets to provide more growth opportunities for American companies and more wealth-building opportunities for the broadest range of American investors.

The SEC is Pushing to Deregulate Public Markets Anyway, Undermining Confidence in Our Markets and Leaving Investors in the Dark

The data is clear that lowering the bar for public company disclosure is unlikely to significantly increase IPOs. Nevertheless, this SEC seems intent on destroying the most fundamental parts of our public company offering and reporting regime with the recent rule proposals discussed in detail below.

a. Deregulating Registered Offerings

In May, the SEC proposed a broad range of changes that upset the historical balance between investor protection and managing costs for companies. These include a number of changes to the Commission’s framework for regulating public offerings. The federal securities laws generally require that companies file lengthy registration statements that go through an in-depth review by SEC staff before a company is able to offer securities to the investing public. This statutory requirement applies to all companies – newly public companies and existing public companies looking to sell additional securities – to ensure investor protection and market integrity. However, the SEC offers some efficiencies to large, established companies with an SEC reporting history, a category called “Well-Known Seasoned Issuers” (“WKSIs”), on the theory that market participants already have sufficient information about these “established” companies to ensure market integrity and investor protection. One such benefit is the ability to use “Form S-3”, a “short form” registration statement that allows companies to (1) incorporate information from its other SEC filings and (2) to time their offerings based on market conditions. WKSIs also qualify to have these registration statements become effective automatically, without SEC staff review, providing flexibility with respect to offering timing. As a result, WKSIs have significant responsibility to be forthcoming and accurate. When the SEC does not review a registration statement in such circumstances, the Commission has less of an opportunity to ensure that disclosures are not misleading, that allowing a company to proceed with the offering is in the public interest, and that the offering is consistent with the protection of investors. WKSIs are also offered other special benefits, including the ability to be able to communicate with investors before a registration statement is filed with the SEC. This existing framework, which offers certain accommodations to large, established public companies, is premised on the market having sufficient information about the company such that the full registration process is not necessary to ensure investor protection.

The SEC’s recent proposal would significantly expand the narrowly afforded exceptions to a much broader population of companies – effectively eliminating the concept of “WKSIs” altogether. Among other changes, the SEC’s proposed registered offering amendments remove key requirements to use Form S-3. The proposal lowers the issuer market cap size threshold, shortens the minimum period during which the company has to have been public, and removes the requirement that the issuer has made required dividend and debt payments. The rule, if implemented, would allow untested issuers, even those who have not complied with their financial obligations, to have instant access to the market without meaningful oversight by the SEC. The SEC is opening the floodgates to an “increase of over 60 percent in the number of issuers eligible” to use Form S-3. The SEC also proposes to eliminate the WKSIs’ market size framework and replace it with a different system of categorization that the SEC estimates would create a 200% increase in the number of issuers eligible for the benefits currently reserved for WKSIs, despite such issuers being neither “well-known” nor “seasoned.” This significant expansion to the WKSI definition is inconsistent with why the SEC created these efficiencies in the first place. Under your proposal, the WKSI exception becomes the rule. The proposed expansion to the WKSI definition would mean that only a minority of companies would be subject to the statutory requirement for full registration statement disclosure and staff review. The result is less seasoned companies are able to take investors’ money with less disclosure and less oversight from the SEC.

In addition to expanding exemptions from the securities laws, the proposal also preempts state securities laws requiring registration for offerings of unlisted securities. Preemption of state registration hinders the ability of state law enforcement to protect investors from wrongdoers – especially as the SEC has had record-low levels of enforcement under your leadership. Under current law, non-listed companies that have not registered with the SEC may still be subject to state-level regulations to protect investors. The SEC’s proposed change would mean that investors in public, non-listed real estate investment trusts and business development companies will no longer have the protections of state registration and regulatory review. The proposed rule also offers registration and communication benefits to business development companies (“BDCs”) and closed-end funds. This loosening of rules for these investment vehicles comes just as BDCs and the related private-credit market experience significant market challenges.

b. Deregulating Public Reporting

As the SEC guts regulations protecting investors from untested issuers, the Commission is simultaneously “reliev[ing] a significant portion of all publicly traded issuers from making a wide variety of disclosures that they are currently required to provide.” The result of this wholesale rollback of required disclosure requirements would almost certainly increase the level of fraud and raise the cost of capital. Under the proposal, accommodations created for smaller reporting companies and emerging growth companies are extended to many more companies — including large issuers with significant market impact. These accommodations result in reduced disclosures on executive compensation, fewer years of audited financials, and eliminating the “say-on-pay” requirement for investors to vote on executive compensation. Eliminating requirements on executive compensation, as required by Dodd-Frank following the Great Recession, appears to be a signature move by the Trump Administration to insulate corporate executives from any accountability or reasonable governance.

The proposal also raises the threshold for qualifying for strict reporting deadlines applicable to the largest companies, making it so fewer companies have to get information to investors expeditiously at the end of a given quarter. Additionally, the proposed rules increase the number of companies that would no longer be required to have auditors reviewing and attesting to their internal controls. Auditors serve as a critical gatekeeper to ensuring that internal controls exist to ensure reliability and accuracy of companies’ financial reports. This deregulatory rule does little to shift the balance of incentives away from raising capital from private capital markets; and only worsens the quality of information and governance in our public markets.

c. Other Deregulatory Proposals

The Commission is also advancing several other deregulatory proposals that amount to an overhaul of longstanding SEC policies meant to protect investors and ensure market integrity.

First, the SEC is allowing public companies to report their earnings to investors less frequently. Since 1970, public companies have been required to report quarterly earnings to investors on Form 10-Q. The SEC’s proposal would upend over half a century of standard practice by allowing companies to report their earnings only semiannually, on a new Form 10-S. As some experts have argued, “U.S. capital markets have remained liquid and robust due in part to investor confidence in the quality and frequency of the information released by companies. A reduction in the frequency of mandatory reporting could result in reduced information flow to investors and less analyst coverage, hampering investors’ ability to make informed decisions, with potentially adverse consequences for the smooth operation of the markets.” Recognizing these concerns, the public has flooded the SEC with a record over 200,000 comment letters, 99 percent of which oppose the rule.

Additionally, the SEC has proposed rescinding the rule it adopted in 2024 requiring public companies to disclose climate-related risks to investors. First proposed in 2022, this rule would have required companies to include in their prospectuses “information about climate-related risks that are reasonably likely to have a material impact on their business, results of operations, or financial condition, and certain climate-related financial statement metrics in a note to their audited financial statements.” Walking back this rule will leave investors with less information about risks to their investment, threatening their ability to make informed decisions and enhance market liquidity. Senator Whitehouse and I sent a letter to the SEC on August 3, 2026, asking the SEC to reconsider the proposed rescission of the climate-risk disclosure rule.

Conclusion

Taken together, your “making IPOs great again” agenda is part and parcel of the Trump Administration’s approach to our financial markets: make it easier for the President’s billionaire donors and corporate executives to avoid accountability or transparency, while leaving regular investors in the dark. Not only will this undermine the reputation of our markets as the most transparent and liquid in the world, but it will also likely fail at its stated goal of actually increasing the number of IPOs and put American investors at greater risk of being defrauded. These proposals should be reconsidered so that the United States public markets can remain the world’s gold standard. I request that this letter be added to the file for the following rules:

? Enhancement of Emerging Growth Company Accommodations and Simplification of Filer Status for Reporting Companies, Release No. 33-11419 (May 19, 2026)

? Registered Offering Reform, Release No. 33-11418 (May 19, 2026)

? Semiannual Reporting Rule, Release No. 33-11414 (May 5, 2026)

? Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules, Release 33-11421 (May 29, 2026)

Sincerely,
